idiom_name: tagged union ({ tag: left | right }) + switch with never default
implementation_notes: The type system expresses Either without a class hierarchy: a discriminated union of two object shapes with a literal tag, plus a switch on the tag, which narrows each branch - and a final arm whose value is typed never proves that no case was forgotten. Nothing checks the shape at runtime, so the constructors and the assertNever helper live in one module and anything arriving as JSON is validated (zod/io-ts) before it is trusted. fp-ts offers the same type with a full combinator set when a library is preferred over hand-written helpers.
pitfalls: Types are erased: a JSON payload typed as Either is neither branch until a schema validates it, and one `as` cast turns the tag into a lie the compiler will then narrow confidently.
Exhaustiveness holds only while the union stays closed - adding a third case is caught by the never-typed default, but a `default: return ""` arm swallows it silently.
An error typed as string pushes callers back to parsing messages: model the reason as a literal union or a class with a stable code and keep the message for rendering.
Structural typing accepts any object with a matching tag, so brands or constructors are needed if the union must not be assembled inline by feature code.
Narrowing depends on the union surviving to the switch: an intermediate helper that widens to unknown/any and returns erases the discrimination the switch relies on.

variants.name: fp-ts Either with pipe-able combinators
variants.implementation_notes: fp-ts defines Either<E, A> as Left<E> | Right<A> with the same Left-as-failure convention, and supplies pipe-able map/flatMap/alt/orElse/match, tryCatch and fromNullable for the boundary with the exception world, and getApplicativeValidation for accumulating validation instead of fail-fast. Choose it when the codebase already depends on fp-ts (or Effect) and you want combinators that are consistent with the rest of the library rather than helpers written per project.
pitfalls: fp-ts is a dependency with its own type-class vocabulary; adopting it for one function leaves the codebase with two idioms for the same outcome.
The combinators are only as safe as the values fed to them: a Left smuggled in through a cast or a non-validated JSON payload is not detected by the types.

Validation and Either look alike but differ in semantics: getApplicativeValidation accumulates errors while flatMap short-circuits, and choosing the wrong one silently changes which failures the caller sees.
